newsitem.title: RUSSIA: Russian govt steps up pressure on Duma over budget.
newsitem.headline: Russian govt steps up pressure on Duma over budget.

text.p: Russia's government on Tuesday gave the opposition-dominated State Duma three weeks to pass a new tax code, raising the prospect that President Boris Yeltsin might otherwise dissolve it.

Rumours of a dissolution, which have angered communist leaders, have circulated for some time. But the pressure moved up a notch when business newspaper Kommersant Daily ran a long interview with acting government leader Anatoly Chubais and said ministers were considering early elections.

"If the 1998 budget were not accepted, the president may dissolve the Duma," the newspaper wrote in the preface to the interview under the headline "Chubais Gives Duma Three Weeks". The new tax code is to form the basis for next year's budget.
The first deputy prime minister, standing in for Prime Minister Viktor Chernomyrdin who is on holiday until June 20, was careful not to spell out the threat in so many words.
"It's not me who dissolves the Duma...That right, according to the constitution, belongs to the president of Russia, Boris Nikolayevich Yeltsin," he said.
"Whether the president will deem it necessary to make use of this right, I will not take it upon myself to predict."
But Chubais, who is also finance minister, reiterated that the new pro-reform government was taking a "tough position" and warned of calamity if the Duma, or lower house, rejected the tax code.
"We cannot wait, the economy and the people cannot wait. That's why we have such a tough position," Chubais said.

The government was "ready to reach a compromise" with the Duma, where communists and their allies make up the biggest group and can block legislation, though have little power to unseat the government without risking dissolution by Yeltsin.

But, Chubais said, a failure by the Duma to conclude its work before the summer recess in three weeks' time would "wreck the whole construction of next year's budget" and jeopardise prospects for the first economic growth since the Soviet Union collapsed in 1991.
The tax code is designed to free business and individuals from complex and often unfairly-distributed taxes, raising more money for the state while encouraging saving and enterprise.

The Duma, which reconvened on Tuesday, has also been dragging its feet on a government bill to slash spending under the 1997 budget to reflect a huge shortfall in tax revenue. On May 23, before its latest recess, it sent the bill back without voting.
The present lower chamber was elected for four years in December 1995, six months before Yeltsin was re-elected president, beating communist leader Gennady Zyuganov.
Yeltsin can dissolve the Duma within a week if, on a confidence vote called by the prime minister, the house fails to back the government. There must then be new elections.
As was shown in 1995, Yeltsin is under no obligation to appoint a government from among the parliamentary majority.
The Duma can also initiate a no-confidence vote, which can result in either the resignation of the government or the president dissolving parliament.

Despite opinion polls showing the unpopularity of the government, the communists and their allies have so far been unwilling to provoke a dissolution. After Yeltsin's re-election, the house voted to re-appoint Chernomyrdin as prime minister.
Zyuganov on Monday warned Yeltsin against a dissolution, drawing comparisons with France, where President Jacques Chirac called early elections only to find his government rejected.
